questions.question: Discuss the psychological impact of system response time and delay on user performance. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Feedback and error prevention
  • Feedback is important because users need to understand how their actions affect the virtual
  • environment.
  • The system can provide:
  • • Visual highlights when an anatomical structure is selected.
  • • Labels confirming the selected organ.
  • • Audio notifications for important training events.
  • • Progress indicators showing the current training stage.
  • • Warnings when the user deviates from a simulated procedure.
  • • A reset option to restore the initial training state.
  • Error-prevention mechanisms should include confirmation for resetting a session, protection
  • against accidental deletion of progress, and clear instructions when tracking is lost.
  • The system should never silently display inaccurate spatial alignment. If tracking becomes
  • unreliable, it should clearly notify the user and suspend any affected precision-dependent
  • training task.

questions.question: Compare remote asynchronous usability testing with moderated in- person usability testing. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Usability, accessibility, and safety
  • The system should be designed to reduce fatigue and mental workload.
  • Usability: Keep frequently used controls accessible and provide a consistent interaction pattern.
  • Accessibility: Support readable labels, sufficient contrast, adjustable text sizes, and alternatives
  • to gesture-based interaction.
  • Comfort: Reduce unnecessary visual movement and provide options to adjust the viewing
  • arrangement.
  • Safety: Distinguish simulated information from real patient data and prevent users from
  • confusing educational overlays with validated clinical guidance.
  • Privacy: Protect medical images and any personal information used during training.
  • Performance: Maintain low interaction latency and reliable tracking so that virtual structures
  • remain aligned with the physical environment.

questions.question: Classify the various human sensory modalities according to their bandwidth and feedback speed in HCI. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Classify the various human sensory modalities according to their bandwidth
  • and feedback speed in HCI.
  • Human sensory modalities are the channels through which people receive information from a
  • computer system.
  • Sensory
  • modality Bandwidth and feedback characteristics HCI application
  • Visual High information capacity; suitable for complex information. Text, images, charts, icons and animations.
  • Auditory Moderate-to-high information capacity for sequential information; rapid alerts. Voice instructions, notifications and spatial audio.
  • Tactile (touch) Useful for immediate physical feedback; relatively limited information capacity. Touchscreens, vibration and haptic feedback.
  • Proprioceptive Provides information about body position and movement. Gesture recognition and motion-based interfaces.
  • Vestibular Provides information about balance and movement. VR motion interaction and movement simulation.
  • Conclusion: Visual and auditory channels are useful for communicating information, while
  • tactile and movement-related senses support direct interaction and feedback. Effective HCI
  • selects the appropriate modality for each task and avoids sensory overload.

questions.question: Illustrate the complete interaction design and spatial user interface (3D UI) architecture for an Augmented Reality (AR) surgical training and anatomical visualization system. / [CO4] [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Illustrate the complete interaction design and spatial user interface (3D UI)
  • architecture for an Augmented Reality (AR) surgical training and anatomical visualization
  • system.
  • Introduction
  • Augmented Reality (AR) is a technology that combines computer-generated information with the
  • real-world environment. In medical education, AR can help students and surgeons understand
  • human anatomy, practise surgical procedures, and visualize internal organs in three dimensions.
  • An AR surgical training and anatomical visualization system overlays virtual anatomical models
  • onto a real patient model, mannequin, or physical training environment. Users can interact with
  • these models through hand gestures, voice commands, touch controls, or tracked instruments.
  • The system must provide accurate spatial alignment, realistic visualization, responsive
  • interaction, clear feedback, and safe training conditions.
